title: Work Statistics of Autonomous Quantum Energy Pumps
abstract: We develop a terminal-resolved theory of work statistics for autonomous quantum energy pumps. By modeling the systems that supply and receive energy as explicit quantum terminals, the energy exchanged with each terminal is defined directly from its Hamiltonian change. When the terminals are modeled by ideal clocks, these full-space observables admit exact representations on the pump Hilbert space and recover the conventional phase-derivative currents of periodically and quasiperiodically driven systems. The framework resolves transported work from energy accumulated in the pump. It also incorporates arbitrary initial pump--terminal correlations and identifies when correlations can enhance directional energy transfer under uncertain driving phases. For periodic pumps, we derive finite-cycle work statistics in Floquet eigenstates, relate their fluctuations to Floquet quantum geometry, and show that the long-time terminal currents become mutually compatible. An exactly solvable two-terminal qubit exhibits noise matching, in which transport becomes sharp through cancellation of common-mode terminal fluctuations even though the individual terminal energies remain noisy. Finally, for physical terminals beyond the ideal-clock limit, we introduce a positive work-variance gap that quantifies the fluctuations missed by a pump-only description. A coherent-cavity benchmark shows systematic convergence toward the ideal-clock regime with increasing occupation while demonstrating that agreement of the mean current alone does not guarantee accurate work statistics.
summary: This paper establishes a comprehensive, terminal-resolved theory for analyzing how work is generated by autonomous quantum energy pumps. By explicitly treating the coupling terminals, it quantifies the role of initial correlations and develops diagnostics like the work-variance gap to measure non-ideal energy fluctuations. It advances understanding beyond mean current measurements in quantum thermodynamics.
main_problem: The research develops a detailed, terminal-resolved theory for calculating work statistics in autonomous quantum energy pumps, moving beyond simple mean current measurements.
main_result: The framework shows that initial pump-terminal correlations can enhance the maximum achievable directional work, and it quantifies fluctuations missed by ignoring terminal backaction via a positive work-variance gap.
method: The theory uses full-space quantum dynamics, tracing over explicit energy terminals modeled as ideal clocks to derive exact expressions for multi-terminal work moments.
model_or_system: The system is an autonomous quantum energy pump coupled to multiple energy sources/sinks (terminals), which are explicitly modeled using clock Hamiltonians. The analysis extends from idealized 'ideal-clock' limits to more realistic, nonideal physical terminals like cavities.
key_observables: Work statistics ($\hat{W}_i(t)$), correlation-assisted gain ($\Delta_{	ext{corr}}(t)$), work-variance gap ($\hat{G}$), and asymptotic current operators ($\hat{w}(\infty)_i$).
important_parameters: Periodicity (Floquet eigenstates), initial pump--terminal correlations, and the deviation from ideal clock behavior.
main_assumptions: Initial models assume ideal clock terminals; later extensions address nonideal physical terminals. The analysis often relies on projecting dynamics onto coordinate-diagonal density matrices ($\hat{\sigma}_P(s)$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the setup, showing a central pump coupled to energy terminals, contrasting idealized quantum clocks with more complex physical terminals like cavities.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the full Hamiltonian and dynamics in terms of terminal couplings, deriving work observables based on these explicit terminals, analyzing the role of initial correlations, applying results to periodic/Floquet systems, and finally extending the theory to nonideal physical environments.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant for AMO and open quantum systems as it provides rigorous tools (like work-variance gaps) to quantify energy flow and dissipation in driven quantum devices beyond simple mean measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of a quantum energy pump coupled to multiple energy terminals. The central pump mediates en- ergy exchange, and the arrows denote work supplied by the terminals. (a) Ideal clock terminals generate the phases of a periodic or quasiperiodic drive. (b) Physical terminals be- yond the ideal-clock limit may include cavity modes, rotors or flywheels, quantum batteries, and other energy-bearing quan- tum systems. Their finite resources and nonrigid dynamics can produce depletion and backaction, while pump–terminal correlations may modify the transfer statistics.

FIG. 2. Phase dependence of the two-clock qubit pump. (a) Cycle-averaged transport current wtr,s for unequal cou- plings (g1, g2) = (0.18, 0.12) and balanced couplings (g1, g2) = (0.15, 0.15). (b) One-cycle standard deviations of the transport work ˆ Wtr, accumulation work ˆ Wacc, and receiver energy gain −ˆ W2 for (g1, g2) = (0.18, 0.12). (c) The same three standard deviations for (g1, g2) = (0.15, 0.15). In all panels, Ω= 1, ϕ1 = δ/2, ϕ2 = −δ/2, and s = −1. The point δ = π in panel (c) is excluded because G = 0 and the Floquet spectrum is degenerate.

FIG. 4. Correlation-assisted one-cycle transport under wrapped-Gaussian uncertainty in the initial relative phase. (a) Maximum attainable mean transport work µmax prod(T) and µmax corr(T) for product and correlated pump–clock prepara- tions. (b) Relative standard deviations of the correspond- ing optimized transport work. The parameters are Ω= 1, (g1, g2) = (0.18, 0.12), δ0 = 2, ϕ1 = δ/2, and ϕ2 = −δ/2. The horizontal axis is the phase width ∆δ.

FIG. 3. Repeated-cycle work statistics and noise matching. (a) Mean transported work and standard deviations versus cycle number for Ω= 1, (g1, g2) = (0.18, 0.12), (ϕ1, ϕ2) = (0.7, −0.8), and s = −1. (b) One-cycle variances for Ω= 1, g1 = g2 = 0.15, (ϕ1, ϕ2) = (π/4, −π/4), and s = −1.

FIG. 5. Convergence of two coherent cavity terminals toward the ideal-clock limit over 1 ≤¯n ≤103. (a) Normalized mean transport Rtr(T). (b) Terminal-induced fraction of the exact transport variance ζtr(T), pump return infidelity 1 −FP (T), and pump linear entropy SL,P (T). The parameters are Ω= 1, (g1, g2) = (0.18, 0.12), (ϕ1, ϕ2) = (0.7, −0.8), and the initial pump state is the lower ideal-clock Floquet eigenstate. The horizontal line in panel (a) marks Rtr = 1; dash-dotted lines in panel (b) are proportional to ¯n−1.
